title: California Expands Privacy Protections by Strengthening Deletion Rights
finding: SB 923, signed September 27, 2026 and effective January 1, 2027, extends the CCPA deletion right to personal data a business obtained from third parties. It also permits suppression lists so that deleted data stays deleted.
atlas_use: Very recent regulation entry; addresses re-acquisition of deleted data. The agency sponsored the bill, so check the enacted text for exact scope.

title: Privacy-Preserving Consumer Rights Requests to Data Brokers
authors_or_outlet: Elina van Kempen; dissertation, eScholarship (University of California)
finding: Brings together the registry-wide compliance studies, reporting that over one-fifth of brokers demand verification for opt-outs. It proposes two systems, PIVA and PIVOT, for private verification and for one request reaching every registered broker.
atlas_use: Summarises the identity-verification problem and points toward better request designs. A dissertation, not a journal article.

title: Data Broker Radaris Loses Domains in Privacy Fight
companies: Radaris | Atlas Data Privacy Corp.
finding: A New Jersey court default judgment in a Daniel's Law suit transferred 14 Radaris-family domains to Atlas Data Privacy Corp. The defendants have moved to vacate the judgment and plan appeals, so the outcome is not final.
atlas_use: Recent status change for the Radaris entry, and an example of private enforcement under a state law. Recheck before publishing because the case is still live.

title: Enforcement Advisory Targets Incorrect Information in Data Broker Registration
companies: SalesIntel Research, Inc.
finding: Announcing Enforcement Advisory 2026-01, the agency warns brokers about incorrect information in registry filings, noting multiple enforcement actions over reporting errors, a $200 daily fine for failing to register, and more than a dozen actions against unregistered brokers.
atlas_use: Important data-quality caveat: the registry is the atlas's likely source, and the regulator itself says some entries are wrong. SalesIntel action ($36,400, 1 September 2026, confirmed): https://privacy.ca.gov/2026/09/calprivacy-continues-enforcement-blitz-with-action-against-virginia-data-broker/

title: Silence Is Not Compliance: Evidence from Two Judicial-Privacy Regimes
authors_or_outlet: Matthew Adkisson, John Muffler; OSF preprint
finding: A search of 87 public broker sites compared a state law with private enforcement (184 suits by September 2026) and a federal law with no publicly reported enforcement found. New Jersey officers who sent requests appeared on 12.5 sites on average, against 62.7 for matched comparison officers. Observational design.
atlas_use: Rare evidence that enforcement design may affect removal. Use aggregates only and label it a non-peer-reviewed preprint.

title: Half a Million Californians Have Signed up for DROP to Delete their Personal Information from Data Brokers
finding: Regulator's figures for the state deletion platform: over 500,000 sign-ups and 654 brokers in the system. Since the 1 August 2026 processing deadline, about 25% of brokers had reported processing requests, though the typical user had been removed by over 40 brokers.
atlas_use: Count of brokers in DROP, and a dated baseline for tracking effectiveness month by month. The figures are self-reported by brokers via the agency, so label them that way.

title: CalPrivacy Brings First Action Against a Data Broker Under Both the CCPA and Delete Act
companies: LocateSmarter LLC
finding: Board decision on a stipulated order with a $116,490 payment for late registration and for allegedly demanding the last four digits of a Social Security number before an opt-out. The agency lists the data sold: names, birth dates, SSNs, contact details, employment and licence data, bankruptcy and litigation information, and inferences such as being litigious.
atlas_use: Enforcement timeline entry and a primary example of opt-out friction treated as a legal violation. Use the primary figure: one secondary source reportedly gives $110,490 (not rechecked).

title: Let My Data Go: Data Brokers' Compliance with Opt-Out and Deletion Requests
authors_or_outlet: Elina van Kempen, Gene Tsudik, Pragya Jhunjhunwala, Mihir Raja; arXiv
finding: Sent opt-out and deletion requests under synthetic identities to all California-registered brokers. Most appeared compliant, but a significant minority did not, many gave no reply, and some demanded intrusive verification the CCPA prohibits for opt-outs. Calls for a standard consumer interface and stronger enforcement.
atlas_use: Complements the access-request study by testing deletion and opt-out directly. The synthetic-identity design is a useful, ethically safer model. Exact rates need the full paper.

title: Privacy Without Remedy: An Assessment of Data Broker Compliance with California Privacy Law
authors_or_outlet: Anna-Maria Gueorguieva, Jennifer King, Apoorva Panidapu, Daniel E. Ho; ACM FAccT 2026
finding: Empirical test of CCPA and Delete Act compliance. Only 9% of 522 registered brokers fully met transparency requirements. In an audit sample of 250 brokers' request processes, 43% made it impossible to exercise all rights and 64% had at least one design feature adding substantial friction. The authors point to decentralized compliance decisions, enforcement limits and regulatory ambiguity.
atlas_use: Headline statistics for opt-out effectiveness, and a replicable audit method. Its registry-based transparency checks could inform per-broker fields in the atlas.
quote: only 9% of 522 registered data brokers were fully compliant

title: GB Group plc full year results for the year ended 31 March 2026
companies: GB Group | IDology
finding: GBG's audited FY26 results record the move from AIM to the London Main Market, completed October 2025. They also say legacy brands including IDology were retired and those businesses now trade under GBG. Acuant is not named.
atlas_use: Fresher evidence that GBG is still listed, and direct evidence that IDology was folded into GBG rather than sold. Acuant remains unresolved by this document. Keyword review, not a full read.

title: Consumer Beware! Exploring Data Brokers' CCPA Compliance
authors_or_outlet: Elina van Kempen, Isita Bagayatkar, Pavel Frolikov, Chloe Georgiou, Gene Tsudik; IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2026
finding: Submitted access requests to all 543 California-registered brokers; more than 40% never responded. Some of those that did respond asked for personal details they had not previously held, so exercising the right created new privacy risk.
atlas_use: Evidence that registry listing does not mean a working rights process, and that verification itself can be a privacy cost.

title: FTC to Ban Kochava and Subsidiary from Selling Sensitive Location Data to Settle Charges They Sold Location Data Linked to Millions of Mobile Devices
companies: Kochava Inc. | Collective Data Solutions
finding: Proposed stipulated order, approved 2-0 by the Commission, in the suit filed in August 2022. It bars sale of sensitive location data without express consent and requires supplier assessments and retention limits; subsidiary CDS has taken over the broker business.
atlas_use: Enforcement entry plus an ownership fact (the broker business moved to a subsidiary). Proposed order PDF, not opened in this check: https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/ftc_v._kochava_-_proposed_stipulated_order.pdf. The release says such orders bind only once the District of Idaho judge signs, so check the docket before calling it final.
quote: unaware of and did not consent to this data sharing

title: Good Luck Opting Out: Manipulative Design Patterns in Opt-Out Processes
authors_or_outlet: Electronic Privacy Information Center (Caroline Kraczon, Justin Sherman)
companies: Acxiom | Experian | TransUnion | Equifax | Epsilon | Cotality | Spokeo | Whitepages | LiveRamp | National Public Data | Venntel | Unacast | X-Mode/Outlogic | Near Intelligence | Nielsen
finding: Audit of opt-out flows at 38 companies, including 15 data brokers, identifying at least eight manipulative design patterns. At least 11 companies required a login or payment before opting out, and at least 15 required multiple separate forms.
atlas_use: Taxonomy of opt-out obstacles for rating broker opt-out pages, and a method to replicate. Companies listed here are the 15 brokers in the sample.

title: Brokering Safety
authors_or_outlet: Chinmayi Sharma, Thomas E. Kadri, Sam Adler; 114 California Law Review 479
finding: Argues that fragmented, repeating broker opt-outs fail abuse victims, because brokers make them easy to locate and removed data reappears. Proposes a system for requesting removal from all brokers at once, and defends it against the industry's First Amendment arguments.
atlas_use: Lead source for why broker-by-broker opt-out fails and for the harm to abuse survivors. Also gives a model for judging centralized deletion.

title: DHS quietly built pathway to track Americans through advertising data economy
companies: PenLink | Cobwebs Technologies | Meta
finding: Pulls together a CBP advertising-ID pilot, a 2023 DHS inspector general audit of commercial telemetry data and the PenLink and Cobwebs merger, with links to primary documents.
atlas_use: Useful pointer to primary records, including the OIG audit and the pilot's privacy analysis, which should be cited directly in the atlas.

title: On the Suitability of LLM-Driven Agents for Dark Pattern Audits
authors_or_outlet: Chen Sun, Yash Vekaria, Rishab Nithyanand; arXiv
finding: The authors built an LLM agent to complete CCPA rights-request flows and classify dark patterns, tested on 456 broker websites. They report on its reliability, failure modes and limits for audits at scale.
atlas_use: Method reference if the atlas's monthly pipeline ever checks opt-out flows automatically, including where automation is unreliable.

title: Lawmakers take pick to ICE's warrantless location tracking purchases
companies: PenLink | Cobwebs Technologies
finding: 70 lawmakers asked the DHS inspector general to examine warrantless location purchases, citing a $2.3 million contract with PenLink for Webloc, which their letter calls no-bid, and a cancelled briefing. A DHS spokesperson later said ICE does not purchase illegal information.
atlas_use: Current government-buyer status, and links to the lawmakers' letter and spending records as primary sources.

title: Deutsche Börse Group to Acquire General Atlantic's Minority Stake in ISS STOXX
companies: ISS STOXX | Deutsche Börse Group | General Atlantic
finding: Deutsche Börse agreed to buy the remaining 20% of ISS STOXX from General Atlantic for EUR 1.1 billion in two payments, with General Atlantic's exit expected at the end of March 2026. That would make it sole shareholder.
atlas_use: Update ISS from majority-owned to wholly owned by Deutsche Börse. The release is forward-looking, so confirm that the March 2026 exit happened before dating it as complete.

title: FTC Reminds Data Brokers of Their Obligations to Comply with PADFAA
companies: LexisNexis Risk Solutions | Exact Data (Data Axle) | Nielsen Holdings | Factual | Clickagy | Skydeo | NextMark | Datasys Group | EproDirect | Complete Mailing Lists | Paramount Lists | Key Marketing Advantage | McGraw (The McGrp International)
finding: FTC sent 13 brokers warning letters under the foreign-adversary data law, listing the covered sensitive categories and penalties up to $53,088 per violation. As warning letters, they are not findings of violation.
atlas_use: A federal list of companies the FTC treats as brokers, useful to cross-check the roster, and the statutory sensitive categories. Recipient list: https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/warning-letters/328666
quote: The FTC is committed to enforcing PADFAA and ensuring companies are complying

title: CalPrivacy Brings New Round of Enforcement Actions Against Data Brokers
companies: Rickenbacher Data LLC (Datamasters) | S&P Global, Inc.
finding: Datamasters was fined $45,000 for failing to register and will stop selling Californians' data; its lists covered Alzheimer's disease, drug addiction and incontinence, plus senior and Hispanic lists. S&P Global was fined $62,600 for failing to register because of an administrative error.
atlas_use: Enforcement entries showing that large and small firms are both caught, and documentary evidence of health and ethnicity-based list products.

title: Verisk Announces Sale of its Marketing Solutions Business to ActiveProspect
authors_or_outlet: Verisk (GlobeNewswire release, read on a syndication page)
companies: Verisk | ActiveProspect | Five Elms Capital | Jornaya | Infutor
finding: Verisk sold Verisk Marketing Solutions, the unit formed from Jornaya and Infutor, to Five Elms-backed ActiveProspect. The syndicated text gives no price.
atlas_use: Move Jornaya and Infutor from Verisk to ActiveProspect. Verisk also hosts the release at s29.q4cdn.com/767340216/files/doc_news/Verisk-Announces-Sale-of-its-Marketing-Solutions-Business-to-ActiveProspect-2026.pdf, not rechecked here, so prefer it as the citation only after a person checks it.

title: WOAH: HUGE TCPAWORLD NEWS AS ACTIVE PROSPECT DEVOURS JORNAYA AND I LOVE TO SEE IT!
companies: ActiveProspect | Jornaya | Verisk | Five Elms Capital
finding: Enthusiastic legal-trade commentary treating the sale as a major development for TCPA compliance, crediting ActiveProspect's client focus and leadership. It gives no detail on changes to how data or consent records are handled.
atlas_use: Context on why the deal matters for TCPA consent records. Treat as commentary, not independent analysis.

title: Big Broker is Tracking You! A Privacy Assessment of Large-Scale Location Trace Datasets
authors_or_outlet: De Boeck, Verdonck, Willocx, Naessens; ACSAC 2025
finding: The authors assessed five location datasets bought from two brokers. They showed that home and work locations can be inferred, identities revealed behind traces, and social graphs built by linking people's traces.
atlas_use: Strong evidence that purchased location data is not anonymous in practice.

title: Clearlake Completes Acquisition of Dun & Bradstreet
companies: Dun & Bradstreet | Clearlake Capital Group
finding: Clearlake closed its purchase of Dun & Bradstreet at $9.15 per share in cash, with the stock delisted from the NYSE. The release names financing arrangers (Ares, Morgan Stanley, Golub, Blue Owl and Clearlake) but no equity co-investors.
atlas_use: Set the ultimate parent of Dun & Bradstreet to Clearlake from 2025-08-26. NetWise inherits this only if it is still a D&B subsidiary; the atlas evidence for that link is the FY2022 10-K, and this release does not mention NetWise.

title: Clearlake Completes Acquisition of Dun & Bradstreet (Form 8-K Exhibit 99.1)
authors_or_outlet: Dun & Bradstreet Holdings, via SEC EDGAR
companies: Dun & Bradstreet | Clearlake Capital Group
finding: The company's own SEC-filed release confirms the Clearlake completion, the $9.15 per-share cash price and the end of NYSE trading.
atlas_use: Primary filing to cite alongside the Clearlake release.

title: Data Brokers Face New Pressure for Hiding Opt-Out Pages From Google
authors_or_outlet: Dell Cameron for WIRED, copublished with The Markup
companies: IQVIA Digital | Comscore | Telesign | 6sense Insights | Findem
finding: After an investigation found at least 35 firms hiding opt-out pages from search results, Senator Hassan wrote to five firms asking about the blocking code, its removal and audit results. Advocates described the practice as a possible dark pattern.
atlas_use: Follow-up timeline for opt-out entries, and a named list of firms that received oversight letters.

title: We caught companies making it harder to delete your personal data online
authors_or_outlet: Colin Lecher and Tomas Apodaca, The Markup/CalMatters (copublished with WIRED)
companies: FourthWall | Kloudend | Telesign | BrightCheck | USPeopleSearch.com
finding: A review of all 499 California-registered brokers found 35 using code that kept certain opt-out pages out of search results. Most did not respond to reporters; two unnamed companies said the code was intentional, to avoid spam.
atlas_use: Directly reusable method: the atlas could run a monthly robots and noindex check on opt-out pages against the state registry.

title: Latham & Watkins Represents CareerBuilder + Monster in Court-Approved Sale Transactions
companies: CareerBuilder | Monster | BOLD | PartnerOne | Iron Corp U.S.
finding: Debtor's counsel reports the bankruptcy court approved a three-part sale: BOLD acquiring the job board business, an Iron Corp affiliate acquiring Monster media properties, and PartnerOne acquiring Monster Government Solutions.
atlas_use: Candidate move of CareerBuilder's job-board operation to BOLD. Whether resume data travels with it, and whether the sale closed, are not stated. Check whether the broker registration still names the old entity.

title: Unbridled and Underregulated: Removing FCRA and GLBA Exemptions from Privacy Laws to Hold Data Brokers Accountable
authors_or_outlet: Caroline Kraczon, Justin Sherman; Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC)
finding: All 19 general state privacy laws passed as of 1 July 2025 exempt FCRA-covered and GLBA-covered data, and 14 also exempt GLBA entities outright, while consumer reporting agencies sell data well beyond credit files. Argues the grey area invites regulatory arbitrage and recommends removing the exemptions.
atlas_use: Best single source for the FCRA and GLBA gap. Its data-level versus entity-level distinction and key-term definitions could be adopted in the atlas's regulation layer.

title: Why Are Hundreds of Data Brokers not Registering with States?
authors_or_outlet: Privacy Rights Clearinghouse, in collaboration with Electronic Frontier Foundation
finding: Cross-matched April 2025 data from five registries in four states (two in California, plus Vermont, Texas and Oregon) into 750 broker groups. Companies registered elsewhere were missing from each state: 291 from California, 524 from Texas, 475 from Oregon, 309 from Vermont. The authors caution that definitional differences mean gaps do not prove illegality, and brokers registered nowhere are not captured.
atlas_use: Directly comparable to the atlas's own registry merge: a benchmark count, a method to check against, and the caveat to carry over.

title: Minnesota lawmaker's alleged killer had list of data broker websites in car, FBI says
authors_or_outlet: Suzanne Smalley, The Record from Recorded Future News
finding: Citing an FBI affidavit, the article reports that police found a list of 11 data brokers in the suspect's vehicle, with notes on which were free and how much information each required. It does not name the sites, and use of them in targeting remains an allegation.
atlas_use: Well-sourced physical-harm case for the people-search category. Word it as alleged and do not infer which sites were involved.

title: Airlines Don't Want You to Know They Sold Your Flight Data to DHS
companies: Airlines Reporting Corporation | Delta | American Airlines | United
finding: Internal CBP documents show an airline-owned data broker sold access to domestic passenger names, itineraries and financial details, and told the agency not to reveal where the data came from.
atlas_use: Strong case for defining brokers broadly enough to include industry-owned clearinghouses, and a clear ownership edge from airlines to broker.

title: Protecting Americans From Harmful Data Broker Practices (Regulation V); Withdrawal of Proposed Rule, 90 FR 20568
authors_or_outlet: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau; Federal Register Doc. 2025-08644 (read on a third-party mirror)
finding: The CFPB withdrew its proposed data broker rule under Regulation V, saying legislative rulemaking was not needed at this time and that it would take no further action on the proposal.
atlas_use: Fixes the current federal status of the FCRA route. Cite the official Federal Register record (the next CFPB item), not this mirror; this entry is a duplicate of it.
quote: legislative rulemaking is not necessary or appropriate at this time

title: Protecting Americans From Harmful Data Broker Practices (Regulation V); Withdrawal of Proposed Rule
authors_or_outlet: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Federal Register 2025-08644, 90 FR 20568
finding: CFPB withdrew its proposed data broker rule under Regulation V, saying rulemaking was not necessary or appropriate at this time and that it would take no further action on the proposal.
atlas_use: Key federal timeline entry. The December 2024 proposal, not opened in this check, is listed as: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/12/13/2024-28690/protecting-americans-from-harmful-data-broker-practices-regulation-v

title: Measuring the Accuracy and Effectiveness of PII Removal Services
authors_or_outlet: Jiahui He, Pete Snyder, Hamed Haddadi, Fabian E. Bustamante, Gareth Tyson; arXiv, listed for PETS 2025
companies: DeleteMe | Mozilla Monitor | Incogni
finding: Participants bought subscriptions to four commercial removal services. The services failed to remove most records they identified, and participants judged only about 41% of those records to be about themselves, pointing to serious accuracy and coverage problems.
atlas_use: Evidence on whether paid removal works, and on false matches in broker data.

title: Cision Affiliate Gets $250m Financing, Extends Debt Maturities
companies: Cision | Castle US Holding Corp.
finding: A Cision affiliate raised $250 million in new financing and pushed maturities beyond 2030 with support from holders of over 90% of its debt. The visible text does not address who owns Cision.
atlas_use: Flag possible lender influence over Cision's ownership. It does not confirm Platinum Equity's current control, which this article does not mention.

title: Corelogic is the latest mortgage industry company to rebrand
companies: CoreLogic | Cotality | Stone Point Capital | Insight Partners
finding: Reports the rename to Cotality and recounts how Stone Point and Insight Partners won the bidding, after Cannae/Senator made a hostile bid and CoStar later bid and withdrew.
atlas_use: Add Cotality as the current name with CoreLogic as an alias, and keep Stone Point and Insight as owners. It shows the owners as of the 2021 deal, not a fresh 2025 cap-table statement.

title: Nearly a Year Later, Mozilla is Still Promoting OneRep
companies: OneRep | Mozilla | Radaris
finding: Mozilla still sold OneRep's removal service a year after saying it would end the partnership. The piece also reports that OneRep appears to be partnered with Radaris, based on reader accounts of Radaris emails promoting it.
atlas_use: Evidence on the limits of removal services. The Mozilla status is dated February 2025 and should be rechecked.

title: The Murky Ad-Tech World Powering Surveillance of US Military Personnel
authors_or_outlet: Joseph Cox and Dhruv Mehrotra, 404 Media (with support from WIRED)
companies: Datastream Group | Eskimi
finding: A letter to Senator Wyden's office names Lithuanian ad-tech firm Eskimi as the upstream source of Datastream's data on military personnel. Eskimi denies involvement, and the collection path remains unclear.
atlas_use: Illustrates opaque ad-tech supply chains and foreign upstream sources. Record the edge as disputed.

title: From "I have nothing to hide" to "It looks like stalking": Measuring Americans' Level of Comfort with Individual Mobility Features Extracted from Location Data
finding: A vignette survey of 1,405 Americans found trajectory features raise more concern than other location-derived features sold by brokers. Some obfuscation raises comfort, and perceptions differ by race, ethnicity and education.
atlas_use: Public-attitude evidence for explaining why location data is treated as especially sensitive.

title: A breach of Gravy Analytics' huge trove of location data threatens the privacy of millions
companies: Gravy Analytics | Unacast | Venntel | Predicta Lab | Tinder | Grindr | FlightRadar
finding: Reports parent Unacast's disclosure to Norwegian and UK authorities and a researcher's count of over 30 million location points in the leaked data. Much of the data reportedly came from ad auctions, and named apps denied direct ties to Gravy.
atlas_use: Confirms the Unacast parent link and the real-time bidding collection route. Keep app names attributed, since those apps denied a business relationship.

title: Texas sues Allstate, alleging it violated data privacy rights of 45 million Americans
authors_or_outlet: Suzanne Smalley, The Record from Recorded Future News
companies: Allstate | Arity | GasBuddy | Fuel Rewards | Life360 | Routely
finding: Texas alleges Allstate and its subsidiary Arity paid apps to embed tracking software and gathered location and driving data on over 45 million Americans, without registering as a data broker. Allstate says consumers consent and that it complies with the law; these remain allegations.
atlas_use: Shows an insurer-owned broker and app-SDK sourcing, and use of a state broker-registration law. Current status not established. The Hunton law firm analysis named earlier was not rechecked: https://www.hunton.com/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/texas-ag-sues-allstate-for-violations-of-texas-privacy-law-in-first-enforcement-action-under-a-state-comprehensive-data-privacy-law

title: Hackers Claim Massive Breach of Location Data Giant, Threaten to Leak Data
companies: Gravy Analytics | Venntel
finding: Report of the claimed breach at Gravy Analytics, parent of government location-data seller Venntel. Hackers claimed to hold customer lists and smartphone location data. The article discusses agencies as users of location data generally, without confirming each as a Gravy or Venntel customer.
atlas_use: Timeline source for the location-data breach, and supports the Gravy to Venntel ownership edge.

title: TechTarget Completes Strategic Combination with Informa
companies: TechTarget | Informa | Informa TechTarget
finding: Counsel confirms the combination of TechTarget with Informa Tech's digital businesses was announced complete on 2 December 2024. The page itself does not state the stake, cash or ticker.
atlas_use: Citation for the completion date. The approximately 57% Informa stake, $350 million cash and TTGT ticker came from earlier search summaries, so verify them against an SEC filing before stating them.

title: FTC Takes Action Against Gravy Analytics, Venntel for Unlawfully Selling Location Data Tracking Consumers to Sensitive Sites
companies: Gravy Analytics | Venntel
finding: FTC alleged the companies sold location data and derived traits covering health decisions, politics and religion, without verified consent, for commercial and government uses. The 5-0 order has an exception for limited national security and law enforcement uses.
atlas_use: Enforcement entry and parent-subsidiary link. The carve-out matters for explaining government access. Final order release, January 2025, not opened in this check: https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/01/ftc-finalizes-order-prohibiting-gravy-analytics-venntel-selling-sensitive-location-data
quote: Surreptitious surveillance by data brokers undermines our civil liberties

title: FTC Takes Action Against Mobilewalla for Collecting and Selling Sensitive Location Data
companies: Mobilewalla
finding: FTC alleged Mobilewalla kept real-time bidding data, including from auctions it did not win, gathering over 500 million advertising IDs with location data and selling segments based on health and religious traits. The proposed order limits auction data to participating in auctions; it was finalized in January 2025.
atlas_use: Shows ad-tech bidstream as a broker supply route, useful for a sourcing category. Final order, January 2025: https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/01/ftc-finalizes-order-banning-mobilewalla-selling-sensitive-location-data
quote: Persistent tracking by data brokers can put millions of Americans at risk

title: Databroker Files: Wie Datenhändler NATO und US-Militär bloßstellen
authors_or_outlet: Sebastian Meineck and Ingo Dachwitz, netzpolitik.org (with Bayerischer Rundfunk and WIRED)
finding: Analysis of a free sales sample of about 3.6 billion location points from up to 11 million devices, supplied by a US broker, exposed movements at US and NATO sites in Germany.
atlas_use: Evidence that a broker's free sample alone can cause harm, and a method model. Published in German.

title: Data Deserts and Black Boxes: The Impact of Socio-Economic Status on Consumer Profiling
authors_or_outlet: Neumann, Tucker, Kaplan, Mislove, Sapiezynski; Management Science 70(11), pp. 8003-8029
finding: Five field tests across 15 brokers show accuracy and coverage depend mainly on who is profiled. Better-off consumers are profiled more often and more accurately. Vendor methods explain almost none of the accuracy differences but do shape who gets profiled.
atlas_use: Shows that broker data quality is unequal across socio-economic groups, which complicates both the accuracy and the coverage narratives.

title: National Public Data Published Its Own Passwords
companies: National Public Data | Recordscheck.net | USInfoSearch | CreationNext | Atlas Data Privacy Corp.
finding: A sister site exposed source code and plaintext credentials in a publicly available archive. The leaked code indicates it queried both National Public Data's database and USInfoSearch, showing data flowing between brokers.
atlas_use: Evidence for a broker-to-broker data-supply edge and for security failures at a small operator.

title: NationalPublicData.com Hack Exposes a Nation's Data
companies: National Public Data | Jerico Pictures Inc. | National Criminal Data LLC | Recordscheck.net | Atlas Data Privacy Corp.
finding: Corrects the widely repeated 2.9 billion figure, which counted rows rather than people; Atlas counted about 272 million unique SSNs. It also traces the operator and related companies through Florida corporate and domain records.
atlas_use: Best source for correct breach numbers and for the operator cluster. Use it instead of the many reports saying 2.9 billion people.

title: Data Defense: Evaluating People-Search Site Removal Services
companies: Confidently | DeleteMe | EasyOptOuts | IDX | Kanary | Optery | ReputationDefender | BeenVerified | CheckPeople | ClustrMaps | Dataveria | Intelius | MyLife | Nuwber | PeopleFinders | PublicDataUSA | Radaris | Spokeo | ThatsThem | Whitepages
finding: Four-month test (May to September 2023) with 32 volunteers, seven paid services and 13 sites: only 117 of 332 profile instances (35%) came down for the 28 participants using services. Manual opt-outs, tested on just four participants, removed 70% within a week, faster than any service.
atlas_use: Best measured evidence for guidance on whether to pay for removal or do it manually. Small sample and 2023 test data, so note both. Press release: https://advocacy.consumerreports.org/press_release/consumer-reports-evaluation-of-people-search-site-removal-services-finds-that-they-are-largely-ineffective/
quote: only 117, or 35%, were removed within four months

title: Data Defense: Evaluating People-Search Site Removal Services
authors_or_outlet: Consumer Reports with Tall Poppy (Grauer, Kauffman, Honeywell per earlier record)
companies: Confidently | DeleteMe | EasyOptOuts | IDX | Kanary | Optery | ReputationDefender
finding: Across seven paid services and 13 people-search sites, only 35% of 332 profiles were gone within four months, with services ranging from 4% to 68%. Manual opt-outs reached about 70% on a small sample of 47 profiles from four participants.
atlas_use: Practical guidance comparing manual opt-outs with paid services, with per-service figures.

title: HireRight Announces Completion of Acquisition by General Atlantic and Stone Point Capital (8-K Exhibit 99.1)
companies: HireRight | General Atlantic | Stone Point Capital
finding: Funds affiliated with General Atlantic and Stone Point completed the take-private at $14.35 per share in cash, ending the NYSE listing. Shares the sponsors already owned were excluded from the conversion.
atlas_use: Set HireRight's owners to General Atlantic and Stone Point, private since 2024-06-28.

title: KrebsOnSecurity Threatened with Defamation Lawsuit Over Fake Radaris CEO
companies: Radaris | Atlas Data Privacy Corp. | Bitseller Expert Limited
finding: Follow-up in which an attorney for the people named in the first report disputes their ownership and places Radaris in Ukraine, while acknowledging the company's listed CEO was a pseudonym invented by its marketing arm.
atlas_use: Must be paired with the March 2024 piece so the atlas records ownership as contested, which also matters for defamation risk.

title: Selling Personal Information: Data Brokers and the Limits of US Regulation
authors_or_outlet: Denise DiPersio; LEGAL 2024 workshop at LREC-COLING 2024, pp. 39-46
finding: Not confirmed beyond the title. The landing page says no abstract is available, so the earlier description of the paper's content could not be supported here.
atlas_use: Possible overview of the US regulatory gap, once the paper itself is read. Workshop paper, so weigh it accordingly.

title: Target Report: Half a Loaf Is Better Than None
companies: Vericast | Valassis | Harland Clarke | RRD | Chatham Asset Management
finding: Print-trade analysis separates what RRD took (digital marketing, the Valassis print business and coupon clearing) from what Vericast kept (Harland Clarke checks and a financial solutions business). It also reports Chatham's 2023 offer for all of Vericast and S&P debt forecasts.
atlas_use: Split the Vericast family correctly: Valassis-derived data businesses to RRD and Harland Clarke remaining with Vericast.

title: The Not-so-True People-Search Network from China
companies: TruePeopleSearch | FastPeopleSearch | CocoFinder | CocoDoc | CocoSign | PeopleFinderFree | Numlooker | FindPeopleFast | Spokeo | BeenVerified | Intelius | The Lifetime Value Co. | PeopleConnect | H.I.G. Capital
finding: Argues that a set of people-search sites with apparently fabricated executives funnels visitors to paid reports from established brokers, apparently for affiliate commissions. The links rest on registration, hosting and recycled stock-photo evidence, and the purpose and China links are suspected. The paid brokers are not accused of running the network.
atlas_use: Supports a distinct 'affiliate funnel' node type separate from data holders, and shows how paid brokers connect to front sites. Mark the attribution as suspected.

title: Lowenstein Represents Chatham Asset Management, Sole Owner of R.R. Donnelley & Sons, in Purchase of Digital Print and Marketing Businesses from Vericast
companies: Vericast | RRD | R.R. Donnelley & Sons | Chatham Asset Management
finding: Deal counsel states that RRD, solely owned by Chatham, agreed to buy Vericast's digital marketing businesses (display, connected TV, social, email) and print businesses (shared mail, inserts, coupon clearing).
atlas_use: Shows these Vericast assets moving to RRD and Chatham. The page never mentions Valassis, so linking Valassis needs a separate source. This is a signing notice; closing not confirmed.

title: CEO of Data Privacy Company Onerep.com Founded Dozens of People-Search Firms
companies: OneRep | Nuwber | Mozilla
finding: Ties a data-removal vendor's founder to dozens of people-search domains through historic WHOIS records and leaked data. The founder acknowledged a stake in Nuwber but denied any information-sharing with OneRep, and said he no longer operates the older domains.
atlas_use: Key evidence for a conflict-of-interest category covering removal services linked to brokers, and for a caveat on opt-out recommendations.

title: A Close Up Look at the Consumer Data Broker Radaris
companies: Radaris | Bitseller Expert Ltd | Centeda | TruthFinder | PersonTrust | Trustoria | Rehold | Difive
finding: Maps a Radaris site network, operated through Cyprus-incorporated Bitseller Expert, by linking shared WHOIS contacts, name servers, phone numbers and mailing addresses. It also reports poor handling of removal requests, and says TruthFinder fulfils reports advertised on Radaris.
atlas_use: Worked template for network attribution, and a source of candidate brand-to-operator edges. Treat each edge as reported rather than proven. Use company links only; the piece also names individuals, who should stay out of the atlas beyond what is necessary.

title: 'Scandal-plagued' data broker tracked visits to '600 Planned Parenthood locations'
companies: Near Intelligence | Recrue Media | AELIUS Exploitation Technologies
finding: Covers Senator Wyden's letter alleging Near Intelligence data enabled ads aimed at visitors to nearly 600 Planned Parenthood sites in 48 states, and alleging resale for national security purposes through a contractor. He also asked regulators to ensure the data is destroyed rather than sold in bankruptcy.
atlas_use: Sensitive-data harm case, plus the question of what happens to data when a broker goes bankrupt. These are a senator's allegations, so attribute them.

title: FTC Order Prohibits Data Broker X-Mode Social and Outlogic from Selling Sensitive Location Data
companies: X-Mode Social | Outlogic LLC
finding: FTC alleged sale of device-linked location data covering clinics, worship sites and shelters, and failure to honour some Android users' opt-outs. The order bans selling sensitive location data and requires deletion of past data unless consented or deidentified.
atlas_use: First FTC settlement with a data broker on sensitive location data, per the release, and a documented opt-out failure. Final order, April 2024: https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/04/ftc-finalizes-order-x-mode-successor-outlogic-prohibiting-it-sharing-or-selling-sensitive-location

title: What to Expect When You're Accessing: An Exploration of User Privacy Rights in People Search Websites
authors_or_outlet: Take, Young, Bhalerao, Gallagher, Forte, McCoy, Greenstadt; PoPETs 2024(4), pp. 311-326
finding: Across 20 people-search sites, access requests mostly failed, and removal was more streamlined but less transparent. Four main groups are behind 14 of the 20 sites.
atlas_use: Direct support for grouping people-search sites by shared operator. Any business-model grouping needs the full paper.

title: Opted Out, Yet Tracked: Are Regulations Enough to Protect Your Privacy?
authors_or_outlet: Zengrui Liu, Umar Iqbal, Nitesh Saxena; PoPETs 2024(1), pp. 280-299
companies: Didomi | Quantcast | OneTrust | CookieBot | National Advertising Initiative
finding: Uses advertisers' bidding behaviour to audit consent. Across four consent platforms and an advertiser opt-out, under GDPR and CCPA, user data was often still collected and shared after opting out, and the opt-out was largely ineffective.
atlas_use: Evidence that ad-tech opt-outs may not stop upstream data flow, plus a bidding-based audit method.

title: Data Brokers and the Sale of Data on U.S. Military Personnel: Risks to Privacy, Safety, and National Security
authors_or_outlet: Duke Sanford School of Public Policy (Sherman, Barton, Klein, Kruse, Srinivasan)
finding: A 12-month study that scraped 533 broker sites built from the Vermont and California registries, contacted 12 brokers and bought from three, through both a US and a .asia domain. Purchased identified records, including health and financial data, cost $0.12 to $0.32 each, and buyer vetting was inconsistent. Location data was available but not bought.
atlas_use: Evidence on price and buyer vetting, and a template for using state registries as a sampling frame. Brokers are anonymised, so it cannot support per-company claims. Sponsored by the US Military Academy.

title: The Delete Act: 'A Fantastically Flawed Attempt At Solving A Critical Problem'
companies: Privacy Bee
finding: Reports criticism from the CEO of Privacy Bee: an undefined consumer 'request' could let brokers claim implied consent, and hashed-identifier matching could miss records over formatting differences. The critic runs a privacy company, so may have a commercial interest.
atlas_use: Lists concrete DROP failure modes to test. Use as a hypothesis source rather than evidence, and disclose the interest.

title: Data Brokers and the Sale of Americans' Mental Health Data: The Exchange of Our Most Sensitive Data and What It Means for Personal Privacy
authors_or_outlet: Joanne Kim; Duke Sanford Cyber Policy Program
finding: Of 37 brokers contacted, 26 responded and 11 were willing and able to sell mental health data, with seemingly minimal vetting of buyers. Prices ran from $275 for 5,000 aggregated records to upwards of $75,000 or $100,000 a year, and one broker advertised names and postal addresses.
atlas_use: Concrete pricing and availability evidence for sensitive data. Brokers are anonymised in the report.

title: Data Brokers and the Sale of Americans' Mental Health Data (PDF)
authors_or_outlet: Joanne Kim; Duke Sanford Cyber Policy Program
finding: Of 37 brokers contacted during a two-month study, 26 responded and 11 were willing and able to sell mental health data. One firm's quotes ran from $0.20 a record down to $0.06 at high volume; another's products ranged from $75,000 to $100,000.
atlas_use: Evidence for the sensitive-data and harms sections, with pricing. It is adapted from an undergraduate thesis, and the sale offers were quotes rather than verified deliveries, so describe it accordingly.

title: Data for Sale: Navigating the Role of Data Brokers and Reproductive Health Information in a Post-Dobbs World
authors_or_outlet: Heather Chong; SMU Science and Technology Law Review 26(1)
finding: Argues that the lack of a comprehensive US law like the GDPR leaves gaps companies use to obtain sensitive health data. Examines how brokers collect and sell it, recent efforts to protect reproductive health information, and the then-proposed ADPPA.
atlas_use: Supports harm and sensitive-category entries, especially reproductive health data. ADPPA discussion is dated.

title: The untamed and discreet role of data brokers in surveillance capitalism: a transnational and interdisciplinary overview
finding: Critical literature review describing the broker industry as under-researched and under-regulated, with threats to privacy, national security and data-market trust. It proposes policy directions including data standardisation, economic incentives, legal definitions of data brokers and an oversight authority.
atlas_use: Orientation map to the literature and a source for definition and taxonomy framing. Its scope goes beyond the US.

title: WereUAt: Location data re-identification from theory to practice
authors_or_outlet: Cyril Miras, LINC, CNIL innovation lab (France)
finding: A regulator's lab obtained a free broker sample of about 100 million location points tied to about 5 million unique identifiers, including advertising IDs, over one week. The database was said to be anonymised, though the article treats it as pseudonymised. This introductory article sets out the project and reports no results.
atlas_use: Regulator-sourced example of what broker location samples contain. It is French, so use as non-US context.

title: Legal Loopholes and Data for Dollars: How Law Enforcement and Intelligence Agencies Are Buying Your Data from Brokers
authors_or_outlet: Carey Shenkman, Sharon Bradford Franklin, Greg Nojeim, Dhanaraj Thakur; OSF record
finding: Based on expert interviews and about 150 publicly available contract documents, it examines federal agencies buying broker data and thereby sidestepping Fourth Amendment and statutory process.
atlas_use: Source for the government-buyer loophole. Its contract-document method could add a buyers layer to the atlas.

title: Senior Advisory Group Panel on Commercially Available Information (declassified report)
authors_or_outlet: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
finding: Outside advisers report that commercially available data now differs in degree and kind from traditional public information, can reveal intimate details and carries counter-intelligence risk. They say publicly available information is no longer a good proxy for non-sensitive information.
atlas_use: Authoritative government source on government as a buyer, and on why 'anonymised' claims should not be taken at face value.
quote: it is often possible (using other CAI) to deanonymize and identify individuals

title: "It Feels Like Whack-a-mole": User Experiences of Data Removal from People Search Websites
authors_or_outlet: Take, Gallagher, Forte, McCoy, Greenstadt; PoPETs 2022(3), 159-178
finding: Qualitative study of 18 people seeking removal, either themselves or through a paid service. They found the process costly either way and hard to verify, and believed aggregators' profits give them a reason to make removal harder.
atlas_use: The human experience behind the compliance statistics, for framing opt-out guidance.

title: Audax Private Equity completes sale of Acuant to GB Group
companies: Acuant | GB Group | Audax Private Equity
finding: Confirms that the Acuant sale from Audax to GBG closed by December 2021, with terms undisclosed, whereas the atlas's evidence is dated at the November announcement.
atlas_use: Replace the announcement-stage citation with a completion source. It shows no later change.

title: What Is the Price of Data? A Measurement Study of Commercial Data Marketplaces
finding: Commercial marketplace listings had a median price of about $1,400 a month for live data products and about $2,200 for one-off static data. Telecoms, manufacturing, automotive and gaming products cost most.
atlas_use: Measured price context for the data trade. It covers marketplaces in general rather than personal data alone, so use with care.

title: Frontiers: How Effective Is Third-Party Consumer Profiling? Evidence from Field Studies
authors_or_outlet: Nico Neumann, Catherine E. Tucker, Timothy Whitfield; Marketing Science 38
finding: Three field tests of more than 90 audience segments across 19 brokers found quality varied greatly and many segments were inaccurate. Identifying a single attribute improved by 0% to 77% on average over random selection.
atlas_use: Cite when distinguishing what brokers claim about segments from measured accuracy. The DOI still needs confirming.

title: Consumer Privacy: Changes to Legal Framework Needed to Address Gaps (GAO-19-621T)
finding: Testimony that no overarching federal law governs private-sector collection and sale of personal data, and that consumers lack a statutory right to learn what is held for marketing. GAO urged Congress to strengthen the framework.
atlas_use: Citable statement of the federal gap for the regulation section. It is from 2019, so pair it with the later CFPB withdrawal and PADFAA.

title: Auditing Offline Data Brokers via Facebook's Advertising Platform
authors_or_outlet: Venkatadri, Sapiezynski, Redmiles, Mislove, Goga, Mazurek, Gummadi; WWW 2019
companies: Acxiom | Epsilon | Experian | Oracle Data Cloud | Facebook
finding: Over 90% of US Facebook accounts were linked to broker data. Controlled ads to 183 US volunteers found that at least 40% of broker-sourced attributes were rated not at all accurate, and financial attributes showed notable inaccuracy.
atlas_use: Key accuracy statistic, and evidence on offline-to-online linkage through ad platforms. The data predates later platform changes.

title: After acquiring Clarity Services, Experian launches alternative-data-driven solution
companies: Experian | Clarity Services
finding: Already the atlas's source. It says Experian's acquisition of Clarity gave visibility into more than 62 million consumers using small-dollar loans, point-of-sale financing and auto title loans.
atlas_use: Keep as is for now. This is not fresh evidence and is no proof of continued ownership, because no dedicated search for later changes was made.

title: Zeta Global acquires commenting service Disqus
companies: Zeta Global | Disqus
finding: Reports the acquisition, with an unnamed source putting the price near $90 million, and frames comment activity as interest data that marketers could target against. It also notes that commenting was declining, so the data's freshness is uncertain.
atlas_use: Evidence for why Disqus matters as a data asset. It is old, so it does not refresh the ownership date.

title: Data Brokers: A Call for Transparency and Accountability
companies: Acxiom | CoreLogic | Datalogix | eBureau | ID Analytics | Intelius | PeekYou | Rapleaf | Recorded Future
finding: Section 6(b) study of nine brokers finding collection largely without consumers' knowledge, buying and selling among them (seven of nine), sensitive inferences and, at some brokers, indefinite retention. It asked Congress for transparency and access laws.
atlas_use: Baseline definition and sector study. Press summary: https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2014/05/ftc-recommends-congress-require-data-broker-industry-be-more-transparent-give-consumers-greater. Several of the nine have since changed hands, so check ownership.
quote: a fundamental lack of transparency about data broker industry practices

title: The Right to Erasure: Privacy, Data Brokers, and the Indefinite Retention of Data
authors_or_outlet: Alexander Tsesis; 49 Wake Forest Law Review 433
finding: A US article on erasure rights and indefinite retention by brokers. Only the repository page was read, and it has no abstract, so the argument is unconfirmed; a PDF is linked there.
atlas_use: Possible foundational citation for the deletion-rights debate in US law, after reading the PDF.

title: Selling Consumers Not Lists: The New World of Digital Decision-Making and the Role of the Fair Credit Reporting Act
authors_or_outlet: Ed Mierzwinski; 46 Suffolk University Law Review (No. 3) 845
companies: Social Intelligence Corporation
finding: Argues online profiling and predictive analytics blur marketing and credit decisions. Many practices presumed outside the FCRA should be brought under it or a parallel regime. Only a truncated excerpt was read.
atlas_use: Early scholarly statement of the FCRA-coverage argument, and useful history behind the later CFPB proposal.

title: The Data-Broker Threat: Proposing Federal Legislation to Protect Post-Expungement Privacy
authors_or_outlet: Logan Danielle Wayne; 102 Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology 253
finding: Only the repository page was read, and it has no abstract. The title indicates brokers threaten people whose criminal records were expunged, and that it proposes federal legislation.
atlas_use: Candidate source for a specific harm: expunged records persisting in broker data.

title: Delinian corporate site
companies: Delinian | Euromoney Institutional Investor | Epiris
finding: Delinian describes itself as the former Euromoney, acquired by Epiris in 2022. The site does not mention Altrata or Wealth-X.
atlas_use: Supports the Delinian-to-Epiris step. The Altrata-to-Delinian link stays unproven by this page, so keep the atlas's parent_review flag and do not treat a footer link as ownership evidence.
